findings.title: load('sotus') returns the nips_model sklearn Pipeline instead of the documented SOTU speeches; hyp.plot(hyp.load('sotus')) crashes
findings.description: hypertools/io/load.py EXAMPLE_DATA maps 'sotus' and 'nips_model' to the SAME Google Drive file ID ('1J0MBhpRwdT2WChfWJ4HXYq6jU4XpyJPm'), so loading the 'sotus' example dataset yields a fitted sklearn Pipeline (CountVectorizer->LatentDirichletAllocation, pickled under sklearn 1.0.2), not the speeches. The load() docstring explicitly says: 'sotus is a collection of State of the Union speeches from 1989-2018.' The cached files are byte-identical (MD5 6a350ab8d85db34e7b924ac8a7f2a19b for both ~/hypertools_data/sotus and ~/hypertools_data/nips_model). The classic text-plotting workflow hyp.plot(hyp.load('sotus')) therefore raises TypeError. examples/plot_sotus.py even contains a workaround comment ("Note: 'sotus' loads a text processing model, not the actual SOTU speeches") -- the example was adapted to the bug rather than the data being fixed. There is a separate, different 'sotus_model' entry (MD5 b885ba9e...), confirming 'sotus' was meant to be the dataset. Fix requires re-hosting/re-pointing the sotus dataset file ID.
findings.repro:
import hypertools as hyp
sotus = hyp.load('sotus')
print(type(sotus))  # <class 'sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline'>
hyp.plot(sotus)     # TypeError
# registry check:
# grep -n "'sotus'\|'nips_model'" hypertools/io/load.py
# md5 ~/hypertools_data/sotus ~/hypertools_data/nips_model
findings.expected: load('sotus') returns the 1989-2018 State of the Union speech texts (list of strings / DataFrame) as documented, and hyp.plot(hyp.load('sotus')) renders the classic text-embedding plot.

sotus type: <class 'sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline'>

findings.title: Static line plots silently resample every trajectory to ~frame_rate*duration (~900) vertices: a 50-sigma single-sample spike in 10,000-sample data is completely absent from the default plot, and the final ~0.1% of samples are never drawn (both backends)
findings.description: plot.py (~line 2328) passes every line-format dataset through interp_array_list(xform, interp_val=frame_rate*duration/(n-1)) even for STATIC plots, so the drawn Line3D always has ~frame_rate*duration (default 900) vertices regardless of input size: 100,000 samples are DOWNSAMPLED to 901 PCHIP-evaluated points. Real samples that fall between the sparse evaluation grid vanish: a random walk of 10,000 samples with a single +50-sigma excursion at t=5001 renders with the spike completely absent (drawn max = walk max; ground-truth matplotlib of the same data shows a dominant needle). A scientist screening timeseries for artifacts/outliers with the default hyp.plot() cannot see genuine extreme events. Additionally the interpolation grid np.arange(0, n-1, 1/interp_val) stops short of the final index: for 10,000 samples the last drawn grid point is index 9987.9, so the trajectory's final ~11 samples (~111 for 100k) are never drawn -- verified by placing +500 on the LAST sample: the 99th percentile of |drawn| coords is 0.920, i.e. the walk fills the normalized box because the endpoint excursion was dropped before axis scaling. The plotly backend draws the same 900-point resampled line (scatter3d n points: 900). The line-smoothing interpolation itself is documented (GH #141) and markers are correctly drawn at true sample points (fmt='.' preserves all 10,000 vertices), but nowhere is it documented that static line plots are LOSSY for n_samples > frame_rate*duration. This is also why large-N line plotting appears so fast in the timing grid (100k+savefig = 0.031s). Borderline-critical: the rendered result silently misrepresents the data on fully-default usage; rated major because the true samples remain available via marker formats and the smoothing behavior is partially documented.

findings.title: duration= and frame_rate= are documented '(animation only)' but silently reshape STATIC plots -- duration=1, frame_rate=2 draws a 10,000-sample trajectory as a single 2-vertex segment
findings.description: Because the static-line resampling target is frame_rate*duration (finding 002), two parameters whose docstrings read 'duration (animation only) : float' and 'frame_rate (animation only) : int or float' directly control static-plot geometry: hyp.plot(d, duration=60) doubles a static line's vertices to 1800, and hyp.plot(d, duration=1, frame_rate=2) renders any trajectory as ONE straight segment with no warning. A user who keeps animation kwargs in a shared kwargs dict and toggles animate=False gets silently degraded static figures. Either the docs must drop '(animation only)' and explain the coupling, or static plots should use a resolution independent of animation timing parameters.

findings.title: align() silently accepts 3D arrays, flattening them into (n_slices, time*channels); on realistic sizes this grinds for ~1 minute and returns meaningless output instead of raising a shape error
findings.description: Passing 3D arrays to hyp.align -- the natural mistake of handing in a (subjects x time x channels) stack instead of a list of 2D arrays -- is silently accepted: datawrangler funnels each (2,100,3) array into a 2x300 frame, and alignment proceeds on 2 'observations' of 300 features, returning (2,300) garbage with no warning. With 2x(2,1000,3) inputs (my spiral-workflow mistake) the same call ran 58.7 s of dense 3000-dim Procrustes before returning, vs 0.049 s for the correct 2x(1000x3) call -- >1000x slower on garbage semantics. reduce/cluster stack-and-fit paths tolerate this less dangerously, but align's row-correspondence semantics make silent flattening especially misleading. An explicit 'expected 2D datasets, got 3D array of shape ...' ValueError would match the module's otherwise-excellent input validation (cf. its exemplary unknown-model and mismatched-rows messages).
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
bad = [np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((2,100,3)) for _ in range(2)]
out = hyp.align(bad)
print(np.asarray(out[0]).shape)  # (2, 300) -- no error, no warning
# slow variant: bad = [np.random.standard_normal((2,1000,3))]*2 -> ~59 s
findings.expected: ValueError naming the offending dataset's ndim/shape and stating that align expects 2D (samples x features) datasets.
findings.actual:
align 3D arrays: ACCEPTED, 0.073s, out[0] shape (2, 300)
[workflow log] W3b align [spiral(2,1000,3) misshaped, rotated]: 58.703s

findings.title: animate.py's 'plays in real time / total ~= duration seconds' claim is 10% off at the default frame_rate=30: PillowWriter emits 30 ms frames, so a 2 s animation plays in 1.80 s
findings.description: hypertools/plot/animate.py comments: 'gif / apng / video writers save EVERY animation frame ... at fps=frame_rate, so an exported file plays in real time: its save_count (== frame_rate * duration) frames at 1000/frame_rate ms each total ~= duration seconds.' Measured on the exported 60-frame gif (duration=2, frame_rate=30): every frame delay is 30 ms (not 33.33 ms), total playback 1.80 s vs the requested 2.0 s -- 10% fast. Cause: the GIF format stores delays in centiseconds, so 1000/30=33.33 ms quantizes down to 30 ms. Frame COUNT (60) and the frame_rate*duration formula are correct. At default settings every exported gif plays ~11% fast; frame rates that divide 100 (e.g. fps=25 -> 40 ms, fps=20 -> 50 ms) are exact. Worth a one-line caveat in the comment/docstring or choosing a centisecond-friendly default.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
from PIL import Image
d = np.cumsum(np.random.default_rng(7).standard_normal((300,10)), axis=0)
hyp.plot(d, animate='window', duration=2, frame_rate=30, save_path='w.gif', show=False)
im = Image.open('w.gif'); im.seek(0)
print(im.n_frames, im.info['duration'])  # 60, 30 -> 1.80 s total
findings.expected: 60 frames x 33.33 ms ~= 2.0 s playback, per the comment.

findings.title: Default animation export (duration=30 x frame_rate=30 = 900 frames) costs 46 s and a 19.7 MB gif for a tiny 300x10 dataset, with no documentation of the cost
findings.description: hyp.plot(data, animate=True, save_path='out.gif') with all defaults renders 900 frames: measured 46.10 s wall and a 19.70 MB file for a 300-sample, 10-feature dataset (vs 3.3 s / 1.55 MB at duration=2). Nothing in the save_path/duration docs warns that a default gif export takes the better part of a minute and ~20 MB. Not superlinear and not a hang -- cost is linear in frame count -- but it is the first thing every tutorial-follower will hit when saving an animation. Suggest documenting the cost in save_path/duration docstrings, or a shorter default duration when save_path is set, or a progress indicator during save.

findings.title: Misspelled/unknown **kwargs to plot() only fail deep inside matplotlib (AttributeError from Line2D.set) after the full reduce/align pipeline has already run
findings.description: hyp.plot(x, bananas=7) raises 'AttributeError: Line2D.set() got an unexpected keyword argument 'bananas'' from inside the matplotlib draw call. The message does name the bad kwarg (usable), but (a) it surfaces as an AttributeError traceback through hypertools internals rather than a hypertools-level error, and (b) validation happens only after the entire (potentially minutes-long on big data) manip/reduce/align pipeline has executed, so a typo costs a full pipeline run. The GH #206 passthrough design makes some late failure inherent, but a cheap pre-flight probe (e.g. validating extra kwargs against Line2D().set before running the pipeline) would fail fast. Plotly backend already handles this better with an upfront warning listing unmappable kwargs.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
hyp.plot(np.random.standard_normal((100,10)), bananas=7, show=False)
findings.expected: Fast, hypertools-level error (or warning) naming the unknown kwarg before the pipeline runs, mirroring the plotly backend's upfront unmapped-kwargs warning.
findings.actual: AttributeError: Line2D.set() got an unexpected keyword argument 'bananas' (raised after format/reduce ran)
